Lessons.Title: Different Square Units (Part 2) — Choosing Square Feet and Square Meters
ExplanationParagraphs: 2021 first-edition Grade 3 U02 L07 follows CCSS 3.MD.C.6. Students distinguish four standard square-area units, specifically recognizing why the larger square foot and square meter are practical for covering substantial surfaces. Area names a two-dimensional region; square meters have sides of one METER and square feet sides of one FOOT. The units are NOT interchangeable, and square inches or centimeters remain suitable for small surfaces.

Warm-up: Notice and Wonder (10 minutes). A publisher photograph depicts a person holding a large square with a playground in the background. Original source photo was visually reviewed for context; Edulytics should present independent line-art/context rather than reuse that photo. Teacher conceals the unit label until learners wonder what could be measured and why a smaller unit would require so many repetitions.

Activity 1: Square Feet and Square Meters (10 minutes). Show or build one 1 m × 1 m square and one 1 ft × 1 ft square. Original learner page separately asks for areas that would sensibly be measured using EACH. Original photos of a girl holding a square meter and a square foot were source-reviewed as scale references but cannot stand in for a physically calibrated ruler. Optional teacher preparation uses rubber bands, four meter sticks and four rulers. Teacher hears pupils justify their context choices rather than marking a numeric answer.

Activity 2: Which Square Unit? (15 minutes). Original Student Task Statements p3 question 1 has six DIFFERENT contexts: baseball field, book cover, classroom, sheet of paper, tabletop and phone screen. For each choose cm², in², ft² or m² AND explain the unit-size reasoning. Multiple defensible estimates may be accepted by the teacher; unit choice is not a uniquely numeric score. Compare a tiny screen with a large school field.

Activity 2 matching exercise (p4 Q2) gives FOUR quantities: about 9 square inches, 3 square feet, 55 square centimeters, and 55 square meters. Match these, respectively, to a playing card, student-desk top, sticky note and classroom floor; independently verify the four unit/quantity correspondences and discuss everyday object size. Each pair can be checked for selecting an expected area, while the reasoning still requires teacher review. Don't confuse a number of square units with square unit side length.

Activity 3: Area Scavenger Hunt (optional, 10 minutes). Students find an object/space for multiple units and record both a chosen unit and reasons, sharing 3–5 observations. The first-edition 2021 HTML teacher lesson says square METERS as the fourth unit. Critically, the publisher's FIVE-page Student Task Statements PDF p5 instead prints square YARDS. Record this genuine PDF/HTML divergence explicitly; a classroom must not silently replace the printed yard request with meters or vice versa. Edulytics provides teacher-reviewed parallel prompts for either documented edition surface, not a bogus agreement claim.

During Activity 2 the original 2021 teacher source names MLR8 Discussion Supports (precise vocabulary and peer dialogue) and Engagement: Recruit Interest (personally meaningful school/community objects). Revisit previously constructed one-inch and one-centimeter units and larger one-foot and one-meter squares. At lesson synthesis ask why it is useful to have multiple area units. Publisher original Cool-down 'Square Feet?' is educator-gated; an independent Edulytics area-unit-choice explanation is used rather than copied wording.

Photos/images are source-referenced by URL and SHA-256 only; no publisher photograph is embedded. Separate first-party simple square outlines illustrate relative side units. Teacher review is required for all open contextual explanations; original printed Student Task Statements five pages checked independently, Stage D and tests intentionally not run.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square meter
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of a square one meter long on EACH side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use m² for large two-dimensional regions, such as fields and room floors.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1-meter-side model represents 1 m², not 1 meter.

KeyConcepts.Title: Square foot
KeyConcepts.Definition: Area of a square one foot long on EACH side.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use ft² for moderately sized areas, such as a tabletop or small patch of floor.
KeyConcepts.Example: A 1-foot-side model represents 1 ft², not 1 foot.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choice of area unit
KeyConcepts.Definition: Pick unit squares small or large enough to tile a given region reasonably.
KeyConcepts.Rule: cm² and in² often suit small surfaces, while ft² and m² suit larger surfaces.
KeyConcepts.Example: A phone screen is more naturally measured in cm² than in m².

KeyConcepts.Title: Printed vs online optional task
KeyConcepts.Definition: Edition surfaces differ in fourth scavenger-hunt unit.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Teacher PDF 2021 p5 requests square yards; online original lesson HTML requests square meters.
KeyConcepts.Example: Keep both explicitly documented instead of claiming exact identical wording.

WorkedExamples.Title: Square units versus sides
WorkedExamples.Question: What is a square meter?
WorkedExamples.Method: Reason about each side of a square.
Steps: Choose a length measuring one meter.
The enclosed surface area is 1 square meter.
Do not answer one linear meter.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 1 m² is the region enclosed by a 1 m × 1 m square.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source six contexts
WorkedExamples.Question: Which unit might fit a baseball field and a phone screen?
WorkedExamples.Method: Match the scale of the region.
Steps: Fields occupy large plane regions: square meters are sensible.
Phone screens occupy much smaller regions: square centimeters are sensible.
Consider whether hundreds or millions of chosen square units would be needed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Baseball field: m²; phone screen: cm² are reasonable examples.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiple plausible units and careful reasoning remain teacher-judged.

WorkedExamples.Title: Four first-edition matches
WorkedExamples.Question: Assign the four areas to the everyday objects.
WorkedExamples.Method: Identify their relative sizes and typical physical areas.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 9 in² → playing card; 3 ft² → student desktop; 55 cm² → sticky note; 55 m² → classroom floor.
WorkedExamples.Check: Digital field can check the four choices; explanations still teacher-reviewed.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional scavenger hunt variants
WorkedExamples.Question: Why do the original PDF and the web lesson name different final large units?
WorkedExamples.Method: Read each original surface without concealing a difference.
Steps: The 2021 public original HTML lists cm², in², ft², m².
The 2021 publisher Student Task Statements PDF page 5 lists cm², in², ft² and square YARDS.
Use the unit specified on the learner's supplied artifact.
Invite learners to explain the scale of both m² and yd² as large-area units.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both variants exist; document which is being assessed.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher chooses and records original source variant; no universal PDF/HTML identity claim.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Saying that a square foot equals one foot.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Foot is linear length; square foot measures covered plane area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show a square measuring one foot along both adjacent sides.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assigning square centimeters to a baseball field without explaining measurement size.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Using very tiny unit squares is unwieldy for such a large area.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Choose larger m² units and explain efficiency.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Marking contextual unit recommendations as single fixed-answer questions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Source Q1 asks learners to justify chosen units, and reasonable alternatives can exist.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use teacher assessment of choice and explanation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Silently treating p5 square yards and online text square meters as identical.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original first-edition student PDF and publisher HTML disagree on that detail.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Document both, assess the surface actually given to pupils.

SummaryPoints: Source primary Student Task Statements is FIVE pages; p2 has two free-response square-foot/metre contexts, p3 six unit-choice and reasoning subparts, p4 four area-to-object matches, p5 optional scavenger hunt.
Main standard units cm², in², ft² and m². Foot and meter require a square, not a single segment.
Source p4 correct matches: playing card 9 in²; student desk 3 ft²; sticky note 55 cm²; classroom 55 m².
Original HTML optional scavenger hunt says square METERS, while original printed PDF p5 says square YARDS; this discrepancy is tracked rather than silently reconciled.
Original three source photos are inspected for instructional context but not reused in first-party lesson media.
Open oral tasks, community observations, physical models and teacher-led MLR8 require human assessment. Only unambiguous area-object matching can be optionally machine-checked.
Regressions authored but not executed; no CI, Stage D, deploy, merge or academic sign-off.
